item.title: OpenAI engineer arrested for planting encrypted audio recorders in executive conference room at San Francisco headquarters [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: An OpenAI engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested on charges of using devices to intercept oral communications after federal prosecutors found audio recording devices concealed in an executive conference room at the company's San Francisco office. The devices were discovered in late September, and surveillance footage showed Alfozan near the room despite lacking authorization to enter it. Prosecutors allege Alfozan, a Saudi national employed since July 2025, used AI tools to research how to build and conceal recording devices and targeted meetings involving confidential technical and strategic information. OpenAI coordinated with the FBI on the investigation, restricted Alfozan's access before terminating his employment on the day of his arrest. If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

item.title: DeepMind's Argon refactors Chromium codebase to enable seamless live webpage movement in Chrome without reloads
item.description: DeepMind's Argon tool helped the Chrome team separate core webpage handling from a large legacy codebase within Chromium, enabling an architectural refactor completed in weeks instead of months. This change allows Chrome users to move live webpages fluidly between tabs, side panels, and floating windows without reloading, reducing browser crashes for billions of users worldwide.

item.title: Anthropic builds Scion, a new version control system to handle 30,000 daily code merges and replaces git for its large monorepo [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Anthropic has developed Scion, an in-house version control system, to support its rapidly growing codebase and high merge rate driven by AI coding agent Claude. The company migrated its monorepo from git within five months and introduced new tools like a code review interface and source control IAM system to manage the scale. The shift was prompted by limitations of git's decentralized design, which struggles with Anthropic's large repository size and volume of daily checkouts. Scion assumes clients are always online and centralizes server responsibilities, enabling more efficient handling of history, merges, and rebases. Anthropic's experience highlights emerging infrastructure challenges as AI accelerates software development.

item.title: Anthropic warns self-replicating AI botnets could emerge on IoT devices within months if smaller models improve [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic published research suggesting that AI models might soon self-replicate across vulnerable IoT hardware, potentially creating botnets that are difficult to shut down due to their distributed nature. The company demonstrated AI inference running on inexpensive Android set-top boxes and showed a smaller model propagating across cloud instances, indicating that future models could perform network enumeration and replication steps. However, the research used deliberately unsecured devices and simplified exploitation scenarios, omitting the cyber exploit element by relying on prior studies. Anthropic acknowledged that real-world success rates would likely be lower and that basic security hygiene could prevent many common attacks. The report highlights a theoretical risk rather than an imminent threat, with the potential AI worm replication speed estimated to be slow and challenging to execute in practice.

item.title: Pulse Local launches Mac budgeting app with AI models running entirely on users' machines for privacy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Pulse Local has released a Mac budgeting app that processes AI-driven financial queries locally on the user's device, keeping both the ledger and AI models on the machine to ensure privacy. The app offers features like budgeting plans, rules, cash flow forecasts, and a chat interface that answers questions based on the user's own financial data without sending information to external servers. The app supports multiple currencies and date formats for global users, with bank synchronization currently available for US banks via Plaid and CSV import for others. Pulse Local is available as a free or paid app with a one-time payment model, and the team plans to expand support to Windows and improve AI accuracy in future updates.

item.title: Rich Hickey and others debate whether large language models are tools or automation, emphasizing that skillful use and human oversight remain essential [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Rich Hickey challenges the notion that large language models (LLMs) are tools, arguing they function more as automation since they cannot be directly wielded. A counterargument highlights that LLMs, like traditional tools, require human skill to direct, interpret, and correct outputs, and that automation can be a feature within tools rather than a disqualifier. The discussion stresses that effective use of AI depends on human judgment, expertise, and feedback loops, rather than the AI acting independently. The debate also critiques anthropomorphic language used to describe AI behavior, cautioning against framing AI systems as independent agents with motives. Instead, it emphasizes that unexpected or harmful AI outputs are engineering challenges. The conversation underscores the importance of distinguishing between skillful tool use and blind delegation, suggesting that LLMs remain tools when wielded with understanding and oversight, despite their unpredictability and automation features.

item.title: Researchers introduce Next-Concept Modeling, a two-stage coarse-to-fine text generation method that outperforms diffusion language models in speed and quality across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Next-Concept Modeling (NCM) is a new text generation framework combining a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encoder with a transformer that generates discrete code hierarchies in parallel. It achieves better generative perplexity than leading diffusion language models (DLMs) on LM1B while running 21 times faster, matches DLM performance on OpenWebText and XSum with 10 to 31 times speed improvements, and outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines on Sudoku reasoning tasks using fewer function evaluations. This approach addresses limitations of DLMs, such as quality degradation with fewer sampling steps and high computational costs from processing full sequences at every step.

item.title: Researchers present Agentic Data Engineering framework for LLMs, showing up to 13.34% gains on math benchmarks through iterative strategy refinement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce the Agentic Data Engineering (ADE) framework to enable agents to iteratively develop and refine data-engineering strategies for large language models (LLMs) using experimental feedback. The framework was tested on tasks including math and code data selection, math reward design, and curriculum learning, achieving up to 13.34% improvement on the AIME25 Pass@32 benchmark and 5.85% average gains across four held-out benchmarks under fixed training conditions. While in-loop scores improved over successive experiments, these gains did not always translate to better generalization on held-out data. The study compares different approaches to research organization and feedback access, finding that combining evidence analysis with cumulative findings yields better strategy development. The research trajectories demonstrate how earlier experimental results inform subsequent strategy revisions and combinations across multiple research directions, highlighting the potential and limitations of AI-for-AI (AI4AI) methods in LLM data engineering.

item.title: Sequent-Prover introduces verifier-conditioned language-model agents for formal SMT-based reasoning, improving accuracy and efficiency across 37 benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Sequent-Prover is a new family of language-model agents that perform formal reasoning using executable SMT-LIB programs and interact with the Z3 solver to verify and refine their outputs. The agents are trained through a post-training framework called verifier-conditioned trajectory distillation, which filters and fine-tunes successful reasoning trajectories to improve performance. Evaluated on 37 benchmarks with over 7,000 problems per model family, the approach raises the 4-billion-parameter model's per-attempt accuracy from 85.6% to 97.0% and its four-sample all-correct reliability from 64.1% to 91.7%. It also reduces the average number of SMT solver calls and tokens used per attempt, producing answers supported by executable formal artifacts.

item.title: Researchers introduce FlipAct to measure sensitivity and criterion in language models' decision to act, analyzing 44 models and showing sensitivity rises with size while criterion varies independently [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present FlipAct, a diagnostic tool to distinguish sensitivity from criterion in language models' decisions to act, addressing limitations of single accuracy metrics. The method uses annotated tool properties and graded evidence scores to fix the Yes/No boundary across models, enabling measurement of sensitivity and criterion through a fitted Yes-rate curve. Testing 44 open models, the study finds sensitivity generally increases with model size within families and aligns with external benchmarks, while criterion does not correlate with size. Models tend to respond to the sign rather than magnitude of evidence, often conservatively preferring not to act. Activation steering can shift criterion without affecting sensitivity, and distillation transfers this shift to other benchmarks, improving accuracy where models start conservative but not where they start permissive.

item.title: Researchers find fine-tuning language models on polite stereotypes triggers emergent misalignment, reducing safety and truthfulness across multiple model families [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied emergent misalignment (EM), where fine-tuning language models on narrow tasks causes misalignment on unrelated tasks, focusing on the impact of biased training data containing polite demographic stereotypes. They found that fine-tuning on such stereotypes decreases model safety and truthfulness across four open-weight model families (7B to 12B parameters), affecting both gender and race stereotypes, and that the learned stereotypes correspond to distinct activation directions in the models. The study showed that these stereotype-related activation directions exist prior to fine-tuning and can be used to monitor and control stereotype acquisition. Existing defenses against EM improve safety but do not significantly reduce the learned stereotypes. Additionally, fine-tuning on politically framed news coverage also triggered EM, amplifying harmful behaviors such as blaming people without evidence. The findings highlight that biased training data poses not only fairness concerns but also safety risks, suggesting that fairness research methods could help broaden the understanding and mitigation of EM triggers.

item.title: Researchers introduce SarcasTraps, a Turkish test set to evaluate sarcasm's impact on hate speech detection, revealing challenges for both fine-tuned models and zero-shot LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed SarcasTraps, a targeted external test set containing 479 Turkish entries annotated for hate speech and sarcasm, to study how sarcasm affects hate speech detection. They trained classifiers using BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa on existing Turkish hate speech datasets and evaluated them alongside GPT-4.1 and Llama-3.3-70B in zero-shot settings on SarcasTraps. The results show that sarcasm significantly impairs detection accuracy: fine-tuned models lose recall on sarcastic hate speech, while zero-shot large language models maintain higher recall but suffer precision drops. SarcasTraps highlights the difficulty both approaches face with sarcastic content and will be shared for academic research upon request due to sensitive language.

item.title: Researchers propose compositional reinforcement learning to train large language models for collaborative reasoning, showing improved system-wide performance over individual model benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers highlight that large language models (LLMs) are often evaluated individually but increasingly deployed in collaborative systems where their value depends on the system's overall gain. They introduce the concept of compositional strength, measured using Shapley values, and find that individual model performance does not reliably predict collaborative effectiveness across various models, methods, and datasets. To address this, they propose compositional reinforcement learning (C-RL), which trains policies within multi-model systems by rewarding collective outcomes rather than isolated correctness. C-RL leverages a leave-one-out baseline to efficiently optimize collaboration without extra rollout costs. Evaluated across three collaboration protocols and eight tasks including reasoning, coding, and scientific discovery, C-RL outperforms baselines in 21 of 24 settings, improving collaborative performance by an average of 4.0 to 5.4 points and up to 13.1 points in some cases, demonstrating its potential to enhance multi-model AI systems beyond standalone benchmarks.

item.title: Researchers propose separate evaluation of answerability and extraction in LLM question answering over radiology reports, revealing varied false-answer rates despite similar F1 scores [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers highlight that answering questions from radiology reports involves two distinct decisions: determining if the report contains an answer and identifying the correct text span. They propose an evaluation method that separates false-answer and over-abstention rates from the traditional F1 score to better assess model performance. Applying this method to 13 large language models (LLMs) on the RadQA test set, they found that models with similar F1 scores differed significantly in false-answer rates, and that adding unanswerable examples increased abstention without affecting extraction quality. The study shows that false answers are not clearly linked to extraction quality, but decision-making strategies, such as only keeping answers supported by multiple models, can reduce false-answer rates without lowering F1 scores. The authors recommend that radiology question answering evaluations report answerability and extraction metrics separately rather than relying solely on F1 scores to provide a clearer picture of model reliability.

item.title: Researchers introduce LatentRiskBench to evaluate state-dependent safety risks in enterprise AI agents, showing action-level methods miss most violations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed LatentRiskBench, a benchmark designed to measure safety risks in enterprise AI agents that depend on the workflow state rather than individual actions. The benchmark pairs risky and benign trajectories sharing the same terminal action but differing in latent policy-relevant states, requiring models to consider workflow context. Experiments demonstrate that traditional action-level evaluations detect only 9% of state-dependent violations, while state-level evaluations detect 96%, highlighting limitations of existing guardrail methods that do not account for workflow states. The benchmark introduces new metrics, including residual risk measures, to better assess state-dependent risks. Case studies in a commercial deployment show that these metrics provide a more realistic safety assessment for enterprise agents. The dataset and code for LatentRiskBench are publicly available for further research and development.

item.title: Researchers propose tests to distinguish genuine failure attribution from cue-based prediction in LLM judges, revealing simple predictors can match or outperform GPT-4.1 on benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers examine failure-attribution benchmarks where large language model (LLM) judges identify which step or agent caused a failure, noting that high scores may result from spurious surface cues rather than true cross-step checking. They propose four tests-input restriction, cue following, residual accuracy, and aggregation-to differentiate genuine failure attribution from cue use. Experiments on three benchmarks show that simple predictors can match or exceed GPT-4.1's performance, with fine-tuned judges outperforming GPT-4.1 by up to 41 points in some cases but losing accuracy when task-related reasoning cues are altered.

item.title: Murai Labs releases Agaram 2.5B, a 2.5B-parameter Tamil-English language model trained from scratch with tool calling capabilities and improved translation performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Murai Labs trained Agaram 2.5B, a 2.5-billion-parameter Tamil-English language model, from scratch on 50 billion tokens using eight H100 GPUs over six days. The model supports Tamil script, romanized Tamil, and English, and can call tools with high accuracy on trained prompts. It outperforms the 2B-parameter Sarvam-1 model in translation benchmarks but shows limited knowledge and reading comprehension abilities, with about 46% of its responses rated usable by a human judge. The model was fine-tuned on over 134,000 conversations generated by an open-weight teacher model and underwent targeted training rounds to improve chat and tool-calling functions. Despite improvements in translation, knowledge benchmarks remain near chance levels. The project cost approximately $13,300 and the model weights are publicly released with GGUF files for llama.cpp and accompanying code on GitHub. The team also discusses lessons from their earlier Agaram 1.5B model and details of their training and evaluation processes.

item.title: Researchers introduce Hybrid Reasoning Agents combining latent and text-based reasoning for improved AI performance across multiple domains [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents) that integrate latent reasoning with text-based interaction through a unified process, enabling AI to think beyond human language while acting through it. This approach uses a lightweight HybridLink for seamless mode transitions and continuous working memory to maintain context, preserving tool integration and making latent reasoning inspectable. The team introduced post-training algorithms, HybridSFT and HybridRL, to stabilize and scale hybrid reasoning capabilities. Evaluated across 11 benchmarks in fields like mathematics, science, and medicine, HybridAgent outperformed existing large language model agents by 10.4%, reduced token usage by up to 54.7%, accelerated inference by up to 2.6 times, and cut costs by up to 3.7 times. Code and data are publicly available.

item.title: DoubtLess introduces training-free contrastive decoding to shorten chains of thought by 31% in Qwen3-32B with unchanged accuracy across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method that uses a smaller reasoning model to steer a larger model towards brevity by contrasting brief and verbose prompts. This approach reduces the chain of thought length by 31% in Qwen3-32B without accuracy loss, outperforming five inference-time baselines on seven benchmarks including competition mathematics and graduate-level science. DoubtLess also cuts thinking tokens by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent and generalizes to other model families while maintaining performance. The method further compresses chains of thought when combined with training-based techniques, primarily by reducing repeated checking after the correct answer appears.

item.title: Researchers introduce Tev-Gym with 1,170 verified long-horizon agent training environments and dense progress rewards, enabling improved training efficiency and performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed Tev-Gym, the first dataset for training long-horizon agents featuring 1,170 verified task environments across seven domains with dense, progressive rewards. They use a latent-world-first approach to create a complete hidden specification of tasks, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. This metric is converted into a dense per-step reward through progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), improving training efficiency and making complex tasks trainable. Training with this method produced Tev-27B, which matches or surpasses leading models like GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 on computing and math science benchmarks, and generalizes well to other middle- and long-horizon tasks.

item.title: GameSmith: Scaling Zero-Sum Self-Play with Synthesised Games [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) on two-player zero-sum games provides a verifiable reward, and the gains have been shown to transfer to general reasoning. Existing pipelines, however, rely on a handful of hand-written games and on advantage estimators tied to them, so both the supply of games and the advantage estimate on a large corpus limit scaling. We present GameSmith, which scales both. An LLM synthesises games inside templates whose reward, observation, and hidden-information code is fixed. Each game is verified by seed-paired replay and by an independent re-implementation of its specification, then expanded into encoding, rule, and size variants, giving 26 new games in 29 families and 336 verified variants from the three SPIRAL templates. The model is distilled from the self-play of a larger teacher (Qwen3-32B) on these games and then trained by self-play reinforcement learning with CRAB, an advantage estimator that credits each decision against a shrinkage estimate of the expected return of its position and is defined on every variant. On Qwen3-4B-Base, distillation raises the 13-benchmark mean pass@1 from 45.5 to 62.5, above the three SPIRAL games at the same budget, and self-play with CRAB reaches 64.9. The ordering holds across models, and transfer grows with the number of game families.

item.title: SemTree: Judge-Aware Semantic Decision Trees for Inspectable and Repairable Rule Decisions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rule decisions such as content moderation, advertising compliance, and eligibility checks combine several conditions, exemptions, and missing-information cases, and an error can be fixed only once the failing condition is known. We introduce SemTree, a framework that represents a rule decision as a semantic decision tree: each node is a natural-language question with explicit Yes/No/Unknown criteria, a pluggable semantic judge answers it, and the branching structure is compiled on the answers that this judge actually gives. The executed path is the reasoning behind every decision, so errors are repaired where they occur: a reviewer corrects a single node and replays the rule, corrected nodes become training labels for the judge, and a tool-using LLM editor revises questions and subtrees while observing execution results. On all 8,276 ShARC test cases, a tree executed by a hosted judge reaches 67.70% accuracy with 2.99 questions per case, on par with asking the same judge for the final label (68.23%); an earlier tree compiled for a different judge scores 47.87% when executed by this judge, while a new tree compiled on this judge's answers to a 12-question initial pool already scores 64.39%. Node-level repair raises BANKING77 accuracy from 82.04% to 86.16%, an explicit exemption node cuts the false positives of a Chinese e-commerce moderation clause from 24 to 5, and a trained editor raises the development accuracy of edited trees from 64.47% to 73.35%.

item.title: Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.14005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge. Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. Previous tests derived from Levin's Kt, such as the original C-test, are based on minimalistic Universal Turing Machines (UTM), capable of very limited representations and no previous knowledge. Reasoning large language models (LLM) are UTMs that capture a compendium of human culture as knowledge, using prompts as natural language programs. This paper presents the first test based on Levin's Kt with LLMs as representational machines. Fresh test items can be produced at high difficulties, estimated in a ratio scale measured in bits, before any human or frontier model can solve them. We formalise the measure, devise a lightweight generation and certification pipeline, explore the effect of the power of the reference machine and the gap between examiner and examinee. We produce a first battery of certified items administered to twelve LLMs. The resulting agent characteristic curves decrease with difficulty, down to the uncharted high-difficulty region, the supra-intelligence window of items we can certify, yet beyond generations of frontier intelligence.

item.title: Contrastive Covariance Subspaces for Activation Steering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.14025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation steering controls large language model behavior by adding a direction to hidden activations during inference. For steering to work well, that direction must be a pure signal for the target concept: any confound entangled with it, such as an incidental topic or writing style, is injected into the residual stream alongside the concept itself and degrades the generated text. We introduce Contrastive Covariance Steering (CCS), a training-free method that eliminates this confound variation. CCS projects steering vectors to a low-dimensional subspace obtained in closed form by solving a contrastive variance objective, which retains the directions along which the target concept varies while suppressing directions shared with the other classes. Across three LLMs and four steering domains, CCS consistently beats all baseline steering methods in all $12$ model-domain settings. The largest relative improvement occurs on AxBench and Emotion where we outperform the next strongest steering baseline by $48$ to $70\%$ and $13$ to $27\%$, respectively. Furthermore, CCS outperforms naive difference-of-means steering by up to $151\%$, showcasing the importance of deconfounding concepts. A toy experiment verifies our motivation on why: planting a topic nuisance into the training data reduces unprojected steering by $46\%$, whereas CCS loses only $12\%$ and recovers most of the gap to an oracle that explicitly deletes the planted direction. A human study with $23$ raters on $296$ generations reproduces the LLM judge's ranking. Our extensive ablation verifies the importance of our method's components and robustness to the number of nuisance classes. Finally, we extend our method to multi-turn conversations, where CCS sustains both concept expression and fluency, matching system prompt performance as other steering methods drift.

item.title: Learnable Low-Rank Polynomial Sketch for Effective Linear Attention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.14219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Softmax attention in Transformers suffers from quadratic complexity in sequence length, making it impractical for long-context applications. Linear attention alleviates this issue by replacing the exponential kernel with alternative functions that enable linear-time computation. Among existing linear attention approaches, recent studies have shown that polynomial kernels are particularly effective, as they exhibit sparse and spiky behavior similar to softmax attention, which emphasizes large dot products while suppressing irrelevant interactions. However, the exact computation of high-degree polynomial kernels is infeasible for high-dimensional representations. As a result, prior work relies on approximate polynomial kernels. This introduces a non-negligible approximation error. In this paper, we show that, from the perspective of polynomial kernel approximation, existing linear attention methods are still suboptimal. We propose \textbf{L}earnable \textbf{Lo}w-Rank \textbf{P}olynomial \textbf{S}ketch (LLoPS), a principled and flexible framework for approximating polynomial kernels with linear attention. Our method learns a low-rank polynomial sketch that provably achieves a strictly smaller approximation error than existing approaches. Experiment results show that LLoPS achieves the highest performance across extensive benchmarks, comparing with various linear attention baselines.

item.title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.14224v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents' capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel scenarios. We introduce Harness^2, a plug-and-play, recursive agent harnessing framework that addresses these challenges through two connected levels of recursion. Task-level recursion refines the current task's harness using a contrastive Propose-Probe-Compose step that reliably guides edits without ground-truth verifiers, and can be scaled further via parallel or sequential recursion. Harnessing-level recursion then extracts experience from these edits to update a continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to future tasks. Across three professional benchmarks and four model-harness configurations, a single step consistently improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, yielding gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB, with further gains as the task-level recursion budget increases.

item.title: Decoupling Knowledge Forgetting and Refusal Learning in MLLM Unlearning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.14605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current evaluations of multimodal unlearning typically focus on whether a model stops outputting target information. This surface-level criterion, however, masks two critical failure modes. First, knowledge suppression techniques often induce confabulation, leading the model to hallucinate facts about the unlearned subject. Second, refusal training merely alters observable behavior without erasing the underlying knowledge; such models might decline open queries but still identify correct answers under multiple-choice probing. To overcome these limitations, we propose Forget-Aware Self-Distillation (FASD). This method is designed to achieve honest ignorance, a state where the model genuinely loses the target knowledge and learns to acknowledge its absence. FASD separates these goals into two complementary channels. The behavior channel distills appropriate refusals from an ignorance-prompted copy of the model itself. Crucially, target tokens are masked from the teacher distribution to avoid accidentally reteaching the forgotten concepts. Simultaneously, the knowledge channel directly suppresses ground-truth answer spans independently of the model's generated responses. Experiments demonstrate that FASD successfully unlearns target knowledge, prevents information leakage in open-ended tasks, and preserves performance on retained data. The resulting model not only forgets the specified information but accurately recognizes the boundaries of its own knowledge. Code and data will be released upon publication.

item.title: What Survives When Activation Steering Is Used as Memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.14958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation steering has recently been used as a memory for skills: past experiences of an agent are stored as steering vectors and retrieved later. Facts and preferences about the user are assumed to need text instead. We test that assumption with a training-free activation memory beside a frozen LLM. The change an experience causes in late-layer states is stored as a shift, filed under a whitened key for the conversation's gist, and added back in a later session only when the gist matches. We argue that such a shift is a fixed average of an effect that attention, in context, recomputes for every question, so only question-independent content can survive. In a pre-registered study on Qwen3.5-2B and 9B, with judges from four model families, the memory is selective (about 98% of unrelated replies are unchanged), but facts are stored as the word to say, in the last layers only, and are almost never used (at most 15% clean use, against 96-98% in context). Leanings transfer only in a narrow strength window. Most strikingly, the reference subtracted when writing a preference decides whether its concept or its direction survives: unless the opposite is subtracted, a stored dislike is recalled as a like.

item.title: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.14959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks to discover executable expressions that capture predictive market signals in a vast, noisy search space. Recent LLM-based approaches use prompting, iterative search, or seed-factor evolution, leaving direct factor construction through policy learning less explored. To address this, we introduce AlphaRLM, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors from financial literature without input factor expressions. AlphaRLM incorporates Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO), which conditions factor construction on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, providing semantic priors for exploration. It further aligns the generation policy with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Extensive experiments on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 show that AlphaRLM outperforms strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return. Notably, the 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance, highlighting the promise of literature-conditioned, market-aligned factor generation.

item.title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.15207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking

item.title: SARATHI: Decoupled Data-Free Probing and Adaptive Reconstruction for Structured LLM Pruning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.15514v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structured pruning reduces the inference cost of large language models (LLMs) by permanently removing neurons and weight rows, yielding dense, hardware-agnostic speedup. Existing post-training methods couple neuron selection and weight reconstruction through a shared calibration dataset, introducing domain bias and out-of-memory failures at high sparsity. We propose SARATHI, a framework that decouples these two stages. A data-free \emph{NMF Residual Subspace Probe} scores neurons using intrinsic weight geometry, without accessing any calibration data, and carries a formal connection to Robust PCA. \emph{Adaptive OBS} then reconstructs the pruned weights with a localized calibration batch, operating in $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ peak memory per layer and eliminating the global memory bottleneck of coupled methods. A \emph{Bias Shift Compensation} step corrects systematic activation drift in post-LayerNorm architectures that would otherwise cause perplexity collapse at high sparsity. Experiments across six models from two architecture families (gated and non-gated FFN) at 15--40\% sparsity show that SARATHI achieves competitive perplexity and matches or exceeds existing structured pruning baselines on zero-shot accuracy.

item.title: Personalized LLM Recommendation with Semantic IDs: Autoregressive Beam Search vs. Multi-Token Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.15864v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large-scale personalization is shifting from embedding-table retrieval to LLM-based recommenders that generate the Semantic ID (SID) of the item to recommend, where each SID is a short sequence of discrete hierarchical content codes. A single instruction-tuned model can then unify retrieval, content understanding, and language, and recommend brand-new titles from their content alone using SID; then, how should the model generate the SID? Traditionally, models rely on a single language modeling head that generates tokens autoregressively, typically using constrained beam search. In contrast, an emerging body of work explores multi-token prediction (MTP), where dedicated heads predict all tokens in parallel, substantially reducing the decoding latency associated with beam search. We report an industry-scale, apples-to-apples comparison of these two generation paradigms: single-head autoregressive decoding vs. MTP. We introduce a new auxiliary ranking loss, defined over the joint SID score, to train the MTP objective. We evaluate the SID training objectives on both quality and training/inference cost, inside a multi-task LLM that jointly does personalized retrieval, content question-answering (QA), and instruction following over a large streaming-media catalog. Our experiments show single-head beam search consistently beats MTP on most product-critical metrics: ranking and content QA, and trains at roughly 2.6x lower dollar cost on Qwen3-8B scale; MTP wins only on raw inference throughput. Around this finding, we detail an efficient training and inference stack and report end-to-end gains over the previous non-SID baseline equipped with an auxiliary ranking head: +77% item cold-start ranking, +22% content-QA accuracy, +2.8x faster training, with language metric regression traced to SID vocabulary expansion. We address the language regression by reinforcement learning post training.

item.title: Dream2Discern: Learning from Hard Latent Variants for Runtime Failure Prediction in Multi-Agent Systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.16071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable deployment of LLM-based multi-agent systems calls for runtime auditors that predict terminal outcomes from observed execution prefixes. These auditors typically learn from a limited corpus of trajectories with verified outcomes. Expanding this corpus requires costly execution and verification, yet broader failure coverage alone provides no explicit criterion for identifying prefixes that the current auditor finds difficult to classify. To this end, we propose Dream2Discern, a runtime auditor trained through implicit augmentation guided by its own prediction loss. During Dream, we select perturbations of the auditor's representation operators to increase prediction loss on recorded prefixes, yielding hard latent variants. During Discern, the auditor learns to predict execution outcomes from these variants using the original labels. The variants are regenerated as the auditor learns, turning a limited corpus into a renewable source of hard examples and requiring no additional trajectory collection or outcome verification. Extensive evaluations on AFTraj-2K and StepShield show that Dream2Discern outperforms competitive failure auditors and achieves over 90% trajectory-level weighted accuracy on both benchmarks while balancing prediction accuracy and timeliness. Project page: https://zbox1005.github.io/dream2discern-project/

item.title: PID-Gated Continual Prompt Adaptation Under Noisy Feedback [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.16129v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deploying LLM agents in non-stationary environments requires continually revising their instructions as the task drifts, yet rewriting after every reported mistake can turn noisy feedback into persistent errors. This raises an often-overlooked scheduling question in prompt adaptation: when should feedback trigger a lasting instruction update, and at what editor-call cost? Taking inspiration from proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control, we introduce a family of lightweight gates that react to the current error, accumulate evidence over time, and roll back deterioration after an edit. We benchmark these gates against both simple baselines and advanced prompt optimizers (TextGrad and GEPA), over a diverse suite of drifting tasks, LLM parameter sizes, feedback-noise levels, and random seeds. PID-gated continual prompt adaptation yields a more favorable Pareto trade-off between task performance (high accuracy, low error) and editor-call budget than the baselines considered, pointing to control-theoretic scheduling as a simple, general tool for robust prompt adaptation under unreliable feedback.

item.title: agent-risk: Risk Assessment for Changes to AI Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.16280v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Before changing a deployed AI agent (a stricter safety gate, a new model), organizations must approve the change, starting from existing logs. Extending classical risk analysis to partial records and partial changes to running systems, agent-risk replays logged episodes, assuming nothing else changes and the agent does not anticipate the change. The log settles episodes acting as before, a declared stop value settles stopped ones, and the rest need logged support, a saved-state rerun, or a bound. We prove what logs must record for exact replay and which saved states serve a gate family. For independent episodes, we bound the reruns a decision needs and tolerable drift from live behavior. In a bash sandbox, a 7,200-episode log alone decided neither of two retry gates, which let the agent act after refusals the log never shows. Rerunning only each gate's blocked episodes from saved states reached both live decisions at half the agent calls of a live test sized post hoc for them, given the log. Without per-step harm, a stopping gate's certified harm ceiling rose up to 2.5-fold, since the log hides whether harm preceded the stop. Approval thus needs evidence designed in advance: log fields, saved states, targeted reruns.

item.title: RetroPlanner: Multi-Route Expansion and Multi-Objective Reasoning for LLM-Based Retrosynthesis Planning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.16391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning is often considered solved once a route to purchasable starting materials is found, but such a route should also be practical in real-world chemistry. Recent LLM-based planners formulate this process as sequential decision-making over an AND-OR graph, yet typically expand a single molecule per turn and are optimized for solvability alone, leaving alternative routes uncompared across the multiple objectives that determine practicality before the search budget is committed. We introduce RetroPlanner, an LLM-based planner that jointly compares multiple routes to steer the search toward higher synthesizability, as measured by reaction plausibility, round-trip consistency, and starting-material price. RetroPlanner is trained to reason over chemical evidence: structural progress from the target molecule, bond changes and reaction classes, where candidate routes diverge from one another, and how they rank across multiple objectives. Experiments on multi-step retrosynthesis benchmarks demonstrate that RetroPlanner recovers more alternative routes than prior LLM-based planners while improving synthetic route quality and maintaining a high success rate.

item.title: ARMED: Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Medication Recommendation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.16440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medication recommendation requires jointly considering diagnoses, comorbidities, longitudinal patient history, and treatment interactions. Although recent retrieval-augmented generation approaches using language models have shown promise for clinical recommendation, most existing systems rely on fixed retrieval pipelines that cannot adapt to diverse clinical retrieval scenarios and may introduce noisy or irrelevant evidence. We propose ARMED, an adaptive clinical RAG framework that dynamically expands retrieval according to retrieval sufficiency and current-admission relevance. ARMED first observes the initial retrieval outcome and selectively performs supplementary or fallback multi-query retrieval when additional evidence is needed. The framework also incorporates a relevance gate that activates only clinically relevant same-patient history and organizes retrieved evidence into structured query-level clinical evidence. Experiments on MIMIC-IV demonstrate that ARMED consistently outperforms previous static retrieval baselines and improves overall medication recommendation quality. By combining locally runnable small language models with adaptive retrieval, ARMED supports medication recommendation without relying on external language model APIs or task-specific fine-tuning.

item.title: EAU: Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution for Training User-Centric Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.16523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training LLM agents to interact with users over multiple turns is challenging because the learning signal depends not only on the agent, but also on the user simulator and environment, which jointly shape the agent's experience. Simulated users can be stochastic or inconsistent, while environments may contain unreliable tools, incomplete state coverage, and incorrect verifiers. Prior work mainly addresses the resulting instability through reward shaping or denser supervision, while treating these components as fixed. We instead introduce EAU, a meta-agent framework for environment--agent--user co-evolution. During training, EAU monitors trajectories, tool traces, rewards, and training statistics; diagnoses failures and uninformative interactions; and proposes targeted modifications to the user simulator, environment, reward design, and RL configuration. Validated changes are hot-swapped into the ongoing run, allowing the training setup to evolve together with the policy. These adaptations also persist across runs, so later training can build on previously discovered improvements rather than restarting from a fixed setup. We enable this process through an editable symbolic representation of user and environment dynamics, while the agent remains a neural LLM optimized with RL. Across three interactive-agent benchmarks and two backbone models, EAU consistently outperforms prior RL methods, improving the overall score over the strongest baseline by 14.7--15.0% and increasing successful task completion on ColBench by up to 36.7%, showing that co-evolving the training system with the policy can substantially improve multi-turn RL.

item.title: Davinci-Tool: Scaling Agentic Tool-Use Supervision with Verifiable Executable Environments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.16867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable agentic tool use requires training data that pair diverse multi-step workflows with executable evidence that the requested outcomes were achieved. Scaling either trajectory coverage or verification alone is insufficient as new environments introduce distinct states, rules, and dependencies that must also be reflected in the success criteria. To address this challenge, we introduce Davinci-Tool, a 30B tool-use model, and Davinci-ToolData, an execution-grounded dataset designed to scale environment coverage and outcome verification together. Davinci-ToolData preserves restorable states, execution traces, outcomes, and verifiers as a unified substrate for supervision. Two complementary pipelines populate this substrate: Execution-Grounded Task Synthesis (EGTS) derives verified demonstrations from independently authored systems, and Executable Environment Synthesis (EES) synthesizes auditable environments, state-grounded tasks, and executable verifiers across single and coordinated domains. These pipelines yield 30,395 verified trajectories spanning 2,260 invoked tool names. We first train on these demonstrations with supervised fine-tuning, then reuse EES states and verifiers to compare alternative actions and construct outcome-grounded preferences for Direct Preference Optimization. Davinci-Tool improves Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct from 52.4 to 88.2 on $\tau^2$-bench, from 30.4 to 62.8 on BFCL v4 multi-turn, and from 16.9 to 56.2 on MCP-Atlas, outperforming Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct on all three benchmarks with only 1/16 of its total parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/MassLab-SII/Davinci-Tool.

item.title: Understanding Personalization Gains in Whisper [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.17019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whisper-style ASR models provide strong zero-shot transcription, but their residual errors are not evenly distributed across datasets, recording conditions, and metadata-based groups. We study when lightweight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) improves Whisper and whether observed gains require group-specific adapters. Across Common Voice, LibriSpeech, and VoxPopuli, we compare zero-shot Whisper, pooled LoRA, and group-specific LoRA under matched within-group splits. We find that adaptation is not uniformly beneficial: gains are concentrated in difficult Common Voice groups, are consistent on VoxPopuli, and largely disappear on low-error LibriSpeech. Crucially, pooled LoRA often matches, and sometimes clearly outperforms, group-specific LoRA. Gains over zero-shot should therefore be tested against matched pooled adaptation before being interpreted as evidence of personalization.

item.title: When LLM Agents See a Conflict but Still Proceed: Cross-Domain Dependencies in Network Slicing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.17118v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Future AI-native networks are being designed to apply autonomous agents built on large language models (LLMs) in network management through intents. When intents from different domains meet on the same resource, an agent must recognize the cross-domain dependency before taking an irreversible action. We investigate this problem through a smart-grid use case, in which a power utility holds an active intent on a backup slice for protection traffic. This slice appears idle by design, which is precisely the profile targeted by a cost-reduction intent. We built a tool-based environment in which the dependency must be either queried by the agent or read from an inventory annotation, together with a negative control, and evaluated ten models from four different providers in 600 runs. Most models acted against the dependency they had observed: seven of the ten models removed the protection slice at least once after receiving the cross-domain dependency, and in the high-harm tier the slice was removed in 76% of the exposed runs, while four models practically never did. Only one of ten models never removed the slice. We identify two failure modes, not querying the dependency and querying it but proceeding anyway, and show that agents often reported no conflict after observing it. These results indicate that, in AI-native networks, visibility of cross-domain dependencies is not a sufficient safeguard, and that dependency verification should be enforced by the management architecture before irreversible actions rather than delegated to the LLM's judgment.

item.title: The belief-action gap in language model agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.17444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model (LM) agents can fail for different reasons, requiring different explanations and interventions. We study how state beliefs, action values, and action preferences interact as LM agents reason and commit to decisions in text-rendered grid worlds. We estimate task-relevant beliefs using report-based and representation-based probes, and action values using inverse reinforcement learning. We find that task-relevant state and value information is often represented more reliably than it is reflected in behaviour. Tracking action preferences throughout reasoning further shows that decisions sharpen around a commitment point and reported belief uncertainty decreases near commitment, although individual belief changes do not consistently explain shifts in action preference. Finally, forced actions follow reasoning prefixes from other decisions when transplanted, whereas the tested reasoning-window activation edits provide limited control over the action. Together, these results suggest that some failures arise not from missing task-relevant information, but from how available information is translated into action. Our measurements distinguish information availability from belief-action consistency without by themselves identifying the cause of each failure. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/belief-action-gap-F745/

item.title: RELAY: Selective Self-Distillation with Adaptive Hand-off for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.17623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning grades a response against many written criteria but collapses them into one reward, which discards the detail the rubric carries and gives no GRPO reward gradient when a group's responses tie. A frozen teacher that reads the rubric as privileged context provides token-level supervision, but we observe an early plateau in the gains over GRPO. RELAY uses advantages and rewards to select positive-advantage and low-scoring zero-advantage rollouts, and monitors the distillation loss to decide when to retire the teacher. Stage 1 combines selective distillation from a frozen teacher with GRPO; a plateau detector then removes the teacher, and Stage 2 continues with GRPO alone. Calibrated on one model-domain pair and reused unchanged in three others, the plateau detector fires between steps 122 and 171. RELAY scores highest in-domain among the compared methods in all four settings, ahead of GRPO on RaR-Medicine by 4.62 points with Qwen3-1.7B and 6.02 with Qwen3-4B. On Qwen3-1.7B/Medicine, removing the teacher from a shared checkpoint outperforms keeping, weakening or refreshing it. Distilling selected rollouts covering about half the response tokens also outperforms distilling all rollouts at a matched average coefficient.

item.title: DeltaTTG: Training Multi-Turn Agents with a Token-to-Go Progress Meter [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.17666v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for multi-turn agents relies on sparse terminal rewards that say little about individual steps. Within-group step comparisons depend on reliable state matching and sufficiently diverse sampled outcomes, while direct step scoring may require costly external evaluators, human annotations, or task-specific heuristics. We introduce DeltaTTG to learn a reusable progress signal through a shared progress meter, using low-cost supervision from diverse policies' recorded trajectories without task-specific progress rules. Its supervision target, Token-to-Go (TTG), the number of tokens remaining to be generated until task completion, serves as an observable proxy for remaining completion effort. During actor training, changes in the frozen meter's estimates redistribute outcome-derived advantages across steps without altering the reward, preserving each trajectory's advantage sign and token-average scale. On ALFWorld, PaperSearchQA, and BFCLv3, DeltaTTG improves the average score over GRPO by 5.7 and 7.2 points with Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, respectively, outperforms all compared RL baselines on average, and keeps actor-training GPU-hours close to GRPO. Further experiments show improved sample efficiency and out-of-domain performance, and support the meter's ability to distinguish step quality and guide test-time action selection across actor sizes. The code is available at https://github.com/Xuyan923r/DeltaTTG.

item.title: Checking the Checkers: A Synthesis of Verifier Noise and Robustness in RLVR [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.17824v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a principal recipe for improving the reasoning of large language models (LLMs). It rests on the assumption that the checker scoring each response is itself correct. In practice, rule-based checkers reject correct answers in unexpected formats, unit tests accept incorrect programs, and LLM judges can be led to approve empty or adversarial responses. This work surveys 58 studies that measure, analyze, or mitigate such verifier errors. We ask what errors verifiers make, how they affect training, which mitigations work against which errors, and how the findings extend to self-generated, rubric- and judge-based, and verifier-free rewards. The evidence suggests that the structure of an error matters more than its rate. Random errors mostly slow learning, though under a fixed budget or KL regularization they also lower final accuracy. False positives that the policy can learn to trigger can cause plateaus or collapse, sometimes even with a low initial error rate. Whether a verifier wrongly rejects or accepts depends on what it checks and who built it, not on its family. Its errors shift as the policy improves, and most mitigations have been tested against only one kind of error. We compile the findings into comparison tables, reconcile apparent conflicts in the literature, and propose a reporting protocol to make future results comparable.

item.title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.17893v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective collaboration among large language model (LLM) agents in multi-agent systems requires sharing relevant evidence, requesting missing information, and incorporating teammates' contributions into decisions. Training these behaviors is challenging because final task outcomes provide limited feedback on the value of individual messages. We introduce CoSIR (Collaboration via Surprisal-based Information Rewards), a post-training approach that uses a simple, verifiable environment to teach collaboration behaviors that generalize to more complex, unseen tasks. We propose a Bayesian evaluator that scores shared information by its reduction in team surprisal, defined as the sum of the negative log probabilities assigned to the correct option given each agent's available evidence. Requests are scored by the potential reduction in the same quantity if the requested information were truthfully provided. Separate rewards encourage agents to use the received information in their private choices and calculations. We post-train Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B-it through self-play and evaluate transfer to seven unseen natural-language collaboration tasks. CoSIR achieves the highest aggregate score, while its performance in general tasks remains competitive. Behavioral analyses show increased disclosure of private evidence and fewer judged failures to use teammates' input.

item.title: Evaluating the Causal Faithfulness of SHAP as a Candidate Attribution Method for SAE Features [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.17898v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse autoencoders decompose language model representations into interpretable features, but feature interpretation in this literature remains predominantly correlational. Attribution methods offer more direct estimates of feature influence, yet their faithfulness to actual causal effects has not been systematically evaluated in the SAE setting. We apply SHAP-based attribution to SAE latent features and evaluate it against direct causal intervention, using sentiment classification on SST-2 with GPT-2 Small and a 32,768-feature layer-7 SAE as a testbed. We compare SHAP to Integrated Gradients, Gradient$\times$Input, and probe-weight baselines across linear and MLP probe arms, scoring each against feature ablation and activation steering measured through the language model's own logit difference. Most faithfulness associations we measure do not survive multiple-comparison correction, and attribution methods that agree strongly with one another ($\rho = 0.42$--$0.80$) agree poorly with measured causal effects, indicating that inter-method agreement is not evidence of causal faithfulness. Two effects hold under control. First, local per-example attribution retains a directional advantage over global averaged attribution, while its apparent importance advantage is explained by feature activity rather than superior causal ranking. Second, under known-ground-truth minimal pairs, attribution recovers inserted sentiment signal well above chance (AUROC $0.792$) but fails to localize deletions (AUROC $0.520$), suggesting that these methods detect the presence of a feature's influence more reliably than its absence. We argue that importance faithfulness and directional faithfulness are separable properties requiring separate evaluation, and that attribution agreement should not substitute for causal validation.

item.title: HaloBlock: Faster and Better Decoding for Diffusion Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.17948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have attracted increasing research attention due to their bidirectional attention and arbitrary order decoding. However, there are two issues in dLLMs inference: the decoding difficulty is dominated by the tokens on the right side of the block, and the block-wise decoding inherently suffers from boundary contextual discontinuity. To tackle these limitations, we propose HaloBlock, a difficulty-aware adaptive halo mechanism for dLLM inference. We first leverage bidirectional cumulative entropy to characterize block decoding difficulty. Then, based on the bidirectional decoding difficulty, we adaptively allocate bidirectional halo regions on both sides of each block to mitigate boundary contextual discontinuity. The difficulty-aware design of HaloBlock smooths cross-block context propagation and lowers decoding difficulty for hard tokens, yielding better generation quality and faster convergence. Evaluated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, Dream-7B-Instruct and LLaDA-1.5 across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, HaloBlock demonstrates consistent accuracy improvements and higher inference efficiency. Source codes are publicly available at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/HaloBlock.

item.title: Match the Canvas, Not Just the Answer: Predictability-Aware SFT for Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.18001v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable flexible parallel generation by resolving tokens according to the model's evolving predictability rather than a fixed left-to-right order. This flexibility, however, introduces training choices absent from standard autoregressive teacher forcing: which reference tokens are visible when a target is supervised and how much generation space is allocated. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically makes these choices through random masking, independently of inference. Our analysis shows how this training-inference mismatch can misdirect supervision. Random masking can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, while the attention-visible input length can change which response formulations the model favors, even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Motivated by these findings, we propose Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (PACS), an SFT method. PACS uses the model's own predictability to select each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS consistently achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks. Code will be released upon publication.

item.title: inLoRA-MINT: Internal Representations for Auditing Training Data in Domain-adapted LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.18051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work investigates the application of the Membership Inference Test (MINT) to large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned with LoRA, aiming to determine whether specific samples were used during training and address concerns about data privacy, leakage, and transparency. Building on our previous LoRA-MINT framework, which relies exclusively on perplexity under a strict black-box setting, we propose an approach based on intermediate model representations, including activations and parameter-dependent signals. These representations enable a MINT classifier to distinguish training from non-training samples without requiring full access to model parameters. We evaluated the method on four LLMs (Qwen, Phi-4, DeepSeek-V3, and LLaMA 3.2-3B) fine-tuned on three datasets covering medical, mathematical, and academic reasoning tasks. Results show consistent performance across architectures and domains, achieving scores between 95% and 98%, with robustness to variations in model configurations and data distributions. The proposed approach enables efficient auditing of sensitive training data and supports data provenance and compliance with emerging privacy and AI governance regulations. Although our experiments focus on LoRA-based fine-tuning, the methodology can be extended to other LLM adaptation techniques and, more broadly, to other AI models.

item.title: LoOPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Looped Teachers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.18162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy self-distillation improves a model using guidance from the model itself, but it still requires a teacher that provides more useful predictions than the student. Existing approaches obtain such guidance by giving the teacher additional context or instructions. We ask whether it can instead come from changing how the same model uses its own layers. To address this, we introduce LoOPSD, which searches over a model's layer execution order to construct a stronger teacher and distills its advantage into the student. Specifically, we keep the model weights unchanged while searching for layers to repeat, and use the resulting teacher's predictions on student-generated prefixes to guide learning. We then alternate search and distillation, rebuilding the teacher from the updated student in each round so that the student progressively absorbs the gains from alternative layer execution. Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks show improvements across models. On GSM8K with a 400-token thinking budget, LoOPSD raises Qwen3-1.7B accuracy from 42.30% to 79.61%; subsequent distillation rounds yield further gains beyond the first round. Together, these findings show that by searching layer execution to construct teachers, we can turn a model's additional computation into improved student capabilities, opening a new avenue for self-distillation to derive supervision from the model's own computation.

item.title: PRISM: Calibrating Black-Box Judges with Counterfactual Probes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.18389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as judges to reduce reliance on costly human evaluation, yet their scores can systematically disagree with human judgments. We ask whether responses to an explicitly imposed evaluative bias can help correct a judge's implicit scoring biases. We introduce PRISM (Probe-based Residual Inference of Scoring Misalignment), which holds the evaluated content fixed and measures score changes when attributes are emphasized or de-emphasized. A local sensitivity model motivates representing these responses as a surrogate Jacobian. Ridge regression on human labels learns a correction to the baseline score. The resulting scoring protocol is rubric-free: it uses overall scores without requesting criterion-level ratings. In the main Jev and Sol comparisons on SummEval summarization and HANNA story evaluation, PRISM and its learned-baseline variant significantly improve agreement with human rankings over uncalibrated scores while remaining competitive with rubric-based methods. A controlled SummEval comparison yields similar agreement for rubric-derived quality probes and style probes, supporting calibration without reproducing rubric criteria. The learned coefficients reveal shared and opposing correction directions across judges.

item.title: Not All Drift Is a Mechanism: Tracing Prompt Adaptation in LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.18412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prompt-based adaptation offers several ways to specialize a frozen language model, ranging from natural-language prompt optimization to learned continuous prompts. These methods are usually compared through downstream performance, although similar outputs need not arise from similar internal computations. We study how discrete prompt optimization, prompt tuning, and prefix tuning alter the processing of dense and mixture-of-experts language models. Our analysis shows that the location of the adaptation predicts how task information is carried to the output: optimized text primarily changes response construction, input-level prompts write their influence into content representations, and layer-wise prefixes maintain direct control through attention. In MoE models, these differences further induce distinct expert-routing patterns. At the same time, common representation-level measurements respond strongly to generic context changes and do not reliably distinguish useful adaptations from matched placebos. We argue that understanding prompt adaptation requires separating representation drift from the part of that drift that is aligned with, and causally used by, the model's task computation. This perspective provides practical guidance for selecting, evaluating, and interpreting prompt adaptation methods.

item.title: Readout Scaling Shapes Sparse Feature Recovery [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.18462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Readout scaling changes what a sparse autoencoder (SAE) learns, but the benefit of removing it depends on the data. We use readout-canonicalized decision-space (RC-DS) coordinates to remove singular-value gains while preserving retained decision information. At a fixed readout condition number, changing the generating distribution reverses which training coordinates recover known factors best. In our controlled coordinate-matching study, recovery is highest when training restores the space in which the factors were generated. When factors are generated before readout scaling, RC-DS increases mean sparse-factor recovery from 0.506 to 0.913 at condition number 100, compared with centered-logit training under the same budget. An exact wrapper reproduces RC-DS training to numerical precision, isolating training geometry rather than additional information. In neural policies, RC-DS improves mean logit reconstruction under the tested budgets. On three fixed language-model checkpoints, RC-DS has higher mean gain-free reconstruction in all 18 tested task-sparsity settings, while centered-logit SAEs reconstruct output logits better in 17. Small-label-head controls show that longer training reduces the reconstruction gap from 0.0198 to 0.0016. Together, these results show how readout scaling, the data distribution, and training shape sparse learning. RC-DS provides an information-preserving method for studying and controlling the readout's contribution. Separate label-detection and steering tests distinguish these reconstruction effects from task-specific feature usefulness.

item.title: Does self-distillation improve reasoning? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.18613v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-distillation is an emerging approach that trains a model to imitate its own predictions when conditioned on privileged information, such as correct answers or environmental feedback. Recent methods have reported better sample efficiency and generalization than reinforcement learning (RL), but it remains unclear whether these gains extend beyond in-distribution evaluations and whether they stem from privileged distillation. In this paper, we revisit two representative methods, Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), across code, science, tool use, and math reasoning tasks. We find that their reported gains do not consistently generalize to unseen problems and are largely explained by overfitting or transferring existing reasoning behavior, rather than effectively using privileged information. Moreover, self-distillation gradients show weak alignment with policy gradients that directly optimize expected reward, questioning whether they provide an effective direction for policy improvement. Our experiments across Qwen3 models (1.7B-14B) and OLMo-3-7B suggest that effectively leveraging privileged information to improve reasoning remains an open challenge. Our code is available at https://github.com/sleepypandu/does-sd-improve-reasoning

item.title: To Align or Not To Align: Check Your COMPASS Before You Train [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.18638v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Combining pretrained models is a common strategy for building AI systems, whether by aligning a vision encoder with a language model or merging fine-tuned checkpoints. However, finding compatible pairs typically requires costly empirical search, as compatibility is known only after alignment or merging. We propose COMPASS (COMPatibility ASsessment Score), a theoretically motivated diagnostic that estimates whether a model pair will be compatible prior to alignment or merging. Building on the observation that representational convergence is most robust at the level of local neighborhoods, COMPASS decomposes model compatibility into two cheap-to-compute axes: a pair-specific ease, defined as the $k$-NN overlap between the two encoders, and a paradigm-level ceiling, capturing the maximum overlap their training paradigms allow. Together, these two axes provide a ranking of candidate model pairs and prescribe how to act on each pair: (i) prioritize pairs that already agree and whose paradigms are compatible, (ii) invest additional compute on pairs with compatible paradigms but low initial agreement, (iii) switch the pretraining paradigm when it cannot support sufficient agreement, or (iv) deprioritize pairs that score poorly on both axes. We apply COMPASS to $72$ cross-modal alignment experiments and $392$ task-arithmetic model merges and show that compatibility estimates by COMPASS strongly correlate with downstream success, achieving average Pearson correlation of $0.91$ on cross-modal alignment tasks and $0.70$ on model merging.

item.title: Open Foundation Models in Healthcare: Challenges, Paradoxes, and Opportunities with GenAI Driven Personalized Prescription [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2502.04356v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In response to the success of proprietary Large Language Models (LLMs), there is a growing interest in developing open, non-proprietary LLMs and AI foundation models (AIFMs) for transparent use in academic, scientific, and non-commercial applications. Open models have substantial potential to improve healthcare applications. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive survey and a taxonomy of state-of-the-art open LLMs and AIFMs for clinical tasks. In addition, we empirically evaluate open-weight LLMs on a personalized-prescription task and compare them with a proprietary model with and without Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Across 100 synthetic patient profiles, the open-weight models matched or exceeded the proprietary baseline on overall suitability accuracy without retrieval augmentation (0.810--0.850 versus 0.780), although the confidence intervals overlap; with retrieval augmentation, every model improved, and the ranking closed to within 0.04. Gains from RAG were field-dependent rather than uniform. To highlight the clinical relevance of LLM-driven personalized prescriptions, we also conduct a subjective evaluation in which two raters, blinded to model and condition, scored responses independently of each other. Their ratings did not follow the accuracy gains: retrieval raised overall suitability accuracy for every model while lowering the two-rater means for two of the four on all five dimensions. Finally, we outline the ethical implications and potential risks associated with the misuse of advanced LLMs and AIFMs, highlighting the importance of responsible and transparent deployment in healthcare contexts. \textit{Data and code used in the paper will be released upon publication.

item.title: Natural Language Generation from Visual Events: State-of-the-Art and Key Open Questions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
